title: Rionegro to the Rooftop: the Cartel, the Barrio, and the Grave at Montesacro
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Rionegro, the birth on the highland road
stops.date_confidence: attested; date and municipality given by en.wikipedia, 'Pablo Escobar'. Coordinates are the town centre; no hospital or house is published, and no civil register entry has been produced by any source consulted.
stops.campa: In Rionegro, in the green hill country an hour east of Medellín, Hermilda Gaviria, a schoolteacher, and Abel de Jesús Escobar, a small farmer, have the third of their seven children. They name him Pablo Emilio. It is a market town of the Antioquian highlands, sitting on the road that carries the city's traffic up out of the valley toward the airport. Thirty-eight years later a Procurador General of the republic will be taken from that road and killed inside this same municipal boundary. No hospital and no civil register entry for the birth appear in anything published.
suggested_refs: Civil register of Rionegro, Antioquia, December 1949, not located in any source consulted

stops.name: Envigado, the school walked out of
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year, 1966, shortly before his seventeenth birthday, per en.wikipedia; month and day unknown and defaulted to 01-01. The quote is tagged [R]: its only citation on es.wikipedia is a Guioteca listicle that carries the line in truncated form and names no broadcast, channel or date.
stops.campa: Shortly before his seventeenth birthday he leaves secondary school in Envigado and does not go back. The town at Medellín's southern edge is where the family has settled, and its own municipal history will later be written almost entirely around him. Accounts of the household divide hard: one line of reporting has him raised in poverty, another has a working family with land, cattle and a schoolteacher's wage coming in every month. Escobar's own version, given years later to a camera, sides with the first. He is sixteen and has no trade.
stops.quote: Pues mi familia no tuvo unos recursos económicos importantes y vivimos dificultades como las que vive la mayoría del pueblo colombiano, entonces no somos ajenos a esos problemas, los conocemos profundamente y los entendemos.
stops.quote_source: es.wikipedia.org, 'Pablo Escobar', citing guioteca.com, '20 de las frases mas recordadas del narcotraficante Pablo Escobar' (23 June 2017); no broadcast named [R]
suggested_refs: The unidentified Colombian television interview from which the 'recursos económicos' line is said to come

stops.name: Medellín, the forged diploma
stops.date_confidence: attested as to substance by en.wikipedia; the year 1968 is the article's approximation and month and day are defaulted. Pin is the canonical Medellín coordinate used across the corpus, not a located university address.
stops.campa: He goes back to schooling with his cousin Gustavo Gaviria, forges a diploma, and enrolls at the Universidad Autónoma Latinoamericana. The money runs out and he leaves without a degree. Gustavo leaves with him, and the two of them will still be working side by side fourteen years later, the cousin as the cartel's second man. No enrollment record for either of them has been located in Medellín. What he tells people in these years is that he intends to become a lawyer and then president of Colombia.
stops.quote_source: biography.com, 'Pablo Escobar' (A&E Television Networks), on his boyhood ambition
suggested_refs: Enrollment records of the Universidad Autónoma Latinoamericana, Medellín, not located

stops.name: Medellín, cigarettes, lottery tickets, and the tombstones
stops.date_confidence: traditional; en.wikipedia dates the petty-crime years to around 1970 without a month. The tombstone story is tagged [R]: en.wikipedia prints it as plain fact and carries no denial, while the family denial reported elsewhere is not in that article. Both versions are in circulation and neither has been withdrawn.
stops.campa: He sells contraband cigarettes and counterfeit lottery tickets in the streets of Medellín and moves into stolen cars. The most repeated story of these years has him and his gang lifting headstones out of cemeteries, sandblasting the inscriptions off and reselling the stone. Encyclopedias print it flat, as a thing he did. Escobar denied it and his mother denied it for the rest of her life, and the denial is not printed alongside. Whether he ever sandblasted a headstone is not a question the record as it stands can answer.
stops.quote_source: guioteca.com listicle of phrases attributed to Escobar (23 June 2017); no original recording or document located [R]
sources: guioteca.com, '20 de las frases mas recordadas del narcotraficante Pablo Escobar'
suggested_refs: Medellín cemetery administration records of headstone thefts, c. 1970, not located

stops.name: Envigado, the Echavarría kidnapping
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, unresolved. en.wikipedia's Escobar article attributes the Echavarría kidnapping and murder to Escobar's gang; en.wikipedia's article on Diego Echavarría Misas dates the death to 19 September 1971 and attributes it to the gang of 'El Mono' Trejos, never mentioning Escobar. Tagged [R] for the attribution, [A] for the killing itself.
stops.campa: The Medellín textile industrialist Diego Echavarría Misas is taken and killed. The family pays fifty thousand dollars and the body is found regardless. In the version that has followed Escobar ever since, this is his crime and the making of his name in the comunas: an industrialist of the old families killed by a boy from the working city, which is a story the working city was willing to hear. In the record kept of Echavarría himself the killing belongs to the gang of a man called El Mono Trejos and Escobar's name does not appear anywhere in it.
suggested_refs: Colombian judicial file on the 1971 Echavarría kidnapping, not located

stops.name: Medellín, the arrangement of the families
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year by en.wikipedia and by Britannica's biography, which gives 'Cartel Headquarters: Medellín (founded 1976)'. No founding month or day exists; 01-01 is a default. Britannica returned 403 on direct fetch this pass and reaches this file through the verified pool only.
stops.campa: With Gustavo Gaviria and the Ochoa brothers he assembles what will be called the Medellín Cartel: coca paste bought out of Peru and Bolivia, refined in laboratories in the Colombian interior, flown north in small aircraft to Florida. It is not a corporation and never has a charter. It is a set of families who agree to share routes, pilots, chemists and gunmen, and who hold to that agreement for fifteen years. At its height the shipments north are estimated at seventy to eighty tons a month. Escobar is twenty-six.
sources: Encyclopedia Britannica, 'Pablo Escobar' (via verified pool; page returned 403 on refetch)
suggested_refs: US DEA and Kerry Committee reporting on Medellín Cartel structure, 1976-1993

stops.name: Medellín, the marriage to María Victoria Henao
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month, March 1976, by en.wikipedia; day unknown, defaulted to 01. María Victoria Henao's own Wikipedia page returned 404 this pass, so the fact rests on the Escobar article and secondary biographies.
stops.campa: He marries María Victoria Henao. She is fifteen and he is twenty-six, and the Church grants a special dispensation for it. She stays married to him for seventeen years, through the congressional seat, through the prison he builds for himself, through the manhunt. She buries him and then spends the rest of her life abroad under another name. Their daughter Manuela is not born yet. Before she is five a car bomb meant for her father will take her hearing.
suggested_refs: Ecclesiastical dispensation for the Escobar-Henao marriage, Medellín, March 1976, not located

stops.name: Medellín, thirty-nine kilos in a spare tire
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month, May 1976, by en.wikipedia; day unknown. The arrest happened on the return from Ecuador and no source consulted names the road, town or checkpoint, so the stop is pinned at the canonical Medellín coordinate and the place is recorded as a gap. The 1977 killing of the arresting officer is tagged [R]: presented as established without a court citation.
stops.campa: Returning from Ecuador he is stopped with thirty-nine kilograms of cocaine hidden inside a spare tire. He is jailed and photographed and the case begins. Money reaches the judges and the case ends. The following year the officer who made the arrest is shot dead, and the killing is attributed to Escobar in every account of his life without a court ever having said so. The method is complete already and will not change for seventeen years. Where on the road he was taken, no published source says.
stops.quote: There have been many accusations, but I've never been convicted of a crime in Colombia.
stops.quote_source: biography.com, 'Pablo Escobar' (A&E Television Networks); no interview date given
suggested_refs: Colombian court file on the May 1976 cocaine case and its dismissal, not located

stops.name: Norman's Cay, the filling station in the Exumas
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the operation and its 1978-1982 span; the 19,000-kilogram figure for the network by the end of 1978 is en.wikipedia's. Escobar's personal presence on the island is not documented anywhere consulted: the island was Carlos Lehder's, and the link to Escobar is cartel-level. Tagged [R] for his presence, [A] for the traffic.
stops.campa: In the Exumas, three hundred kilometres off the Florida coast, Carlos Lehder buys up an island with an airstrip and turns it into a filling station for cocaine: small planes out of Colombia refuelled, reloaded and sent on to the keys and the swamps behind Miami. By the end of 1978 the network has moved an estimated nineteen thousand kilograms into the United States. Bahamian pressure closes the island around 1982. Escobar is not documented on the cay at any point. The traffic through it is his.
suggested_refs: US indictment and trial record of Carlos Lehder, 1987-1988, for the Norman's Cay operation

stops.name: Puerto Triunfo, Hacienda Nápoles
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia, 'Hacienda Nápoles' gives 1979 for the building of the estate and 5 degrees 54 minutes 52 seconds north, 74 degrees 43 minutes 18 seconds west for its coordinates, used here. Month and day defaulted. The verified pool carried a second coordinate roughly 11 km southeast which is wrong and is not used.
stops.campa: On twenty square kilometres of the Magdalena valley between Puerto Triunfo and Doradal he raises an estate with a private airstrip, a bullring, a Formula One track, a sculpture park, and a zoo stocked with elephants, giraffes, zebras and four hippopotamuses shipped in from abroad. Families drive out from Medellín on Sundays to look at the animals through the fence, and are not turned away. Over the gate, where another man would put a coat of arms, he mounts a Piper Super Cub, the aeroplane of his first smuggling run.
suggested_refs: The Piper Super Cub mounted over the gate of Hacienda Nápoles

stops.name: Miami Beach, the house on North Bay Road
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The address 5860 North Bay Road, Miami Beach is real and geocodes to 25.8404, -80.1323 per OpenStreetMap; the coordinate carried in the verified pool was 0.9 km off and is corrected here. The '6,500 square feet' figure and the Britannica attribution could not be reverified, Britannica returning 403. Year is a decade default.
stops.campa: On the water at 5860 North Bay Road he holds a mansion on Biscayne Bay, one node in a property network built out of the American appetite the cartel feeds. Griselda Blanco, out of Medellín a generation before him, opened these routes and taught this city the killing from the back of a motorcycle, and his cartel takes the routes over. Miami in these years is the receiving end. The money comes back through it in cash, and the killings that come with the trade are done in its parking lots and on its causeways.
sources: Encyclopedia Britannica, 'Pablo Escobar' (via verified pool; 403 on refetch)
OpenStreetMap geocoding of 5860 North Bay Road, Miami Beach FL 33140
griselda_blanco.journey.json, stops 'Medellín, brought up into the valley' and 'Miami, three thousand four hundred pounds a month'
suggested_refs: Miami-Dade County property records for 5860 North Bay Road

stops.name: Isla Grande, the second sea
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, single source. The holding on Isla Grande in the Islas del Rosario is reported in Britannica's biography and nowhere documented with a deed in anything consulted; Britannica returned 403 on refetch this pass. Decade only, defaulted to 1980-01-01.
stops.campa: On Isla Grande, in the Islas del Rosario some thirty-five kilometres off Cartagena, he holds a second Caribbean property. The archipelago is coral and mangrove and shallow clear water, of no strategic use to a trafficker whatever: not a runway, not a laboratory, not a route. By this point in the accounts the money has stopped being counted and started being spent, and properties appear in the reference literature faster than any registry can be made to confirm them. This one is named and not documented.
sources: Encyclopedia Britannica, 'Pablo Escobar' (via verified pool; 403 on refetch)
suggested_refs: Colombian asset-forfeiture inventories of Escobar properties in the Islas del Rosario

stops.name: Puerto Boyacá, Death to Kidnappers
stops.date_confidence: attested by en.wikipedia, 'Muerte a Secuestradores'; sources give 1981 and 1982 for the founding and the verified pool carried both. Month and day defaulted. The Martha Nieves Ochoa kidnapping is the stated trigger in the same article.
stops.campa: Guerrillas kidnap Martha Nieves Ochoa, sister of Escobar's partners in the cartel. The traffickers do not pay. They meet instead in the Magdalena Medio, at Puerto Boyacá, with army officers, politicians and cattle landowners, and found Muerte a Secuestradores, Death to Kidnappers. It is the first time the cocaine money and the counterinsurgency apparatus of the Colombian state sit down at one table, and the paramilitary structures of the next thirty years come out of that room. Within a year the organisation is operating in eight departments.
suggested_refs: Colombian Procuraduría investigation into MAS membership among serving military officers, 1983

stops.name: Bogotá, sworn in at the Capitolio
stops.date_confidence: attested; Britannica's biography gives the term as 20 July 1982 to 26 October 1983 for the Medellín constituency, and en.wikipedia records the alternate seat, the parliamentary immunity and the diplomatic passport. Britannica returned 403 on refetch and reaches this file through the verified pool.
stops.campa: On the twentieth of July he is sworn in at the Capitolio Nacional on the Plaza de Bolívar, an alternate member of the Chamber of Representatives for Medellín, elected on a Liberal list. The seat carries parliamentary immunity and a diplomatic passport. He sits in the legislature of a republic whose extradition treaty with the United States is the single thing he fears, and he sits there lawfully, and the press photographs him doing it. He holds the seat until the twenty-sixth of October 1983.
stops.quote: Yo soy un exportador de flores que generó su fortuna vendiendo carros.
stops.quote_source: Interview with Elizabeth Mora, then of El Tiempo, conducted 1984, shelved unpublished after the Lara Bonilla assassination and finally published February 2025 by El Reverbero; reported by Infobae. Infobae renders the phrases in reported speech, so the single sentence is a compression.
sources: Encyclopedia Britannica, 'Pablo Escobar' (via verified pool; 403 on refetch)
es.wikiquote.org, 'Pablo Escobar', citing Infobae on the Mora interview
suggested_refs: The 1984 Elizabeth Mora interview, published February 2025 by El Reverbero

stops.name: Medellín, the barrio built out of the dump
stops.date_confidence: attested; es.wikipedia, 'Barrio Pablo Escobar' gives 1984, the Medellín sin Tugurios program, 250 initial houses and the families from the Moravia garbage dump. Month and day defaulted. Coordinate corrected to Comuna 9 (Buenos Aires) per OpenStreetMap; the verified pool carried a second value 3.6 km west, on the wrong side of the river. The 'sixty soccer fields' figure could not be sourced and is dropped.
stops.campa: In the eastern comunas he funds two hundred and fifty houses for families living on the garbage dump at Moravia, under a program he names Medellín sin Tugurios, Medellín Without Slums. The state's official name for the settlement is Loreto. Nobody uses it. It grows to four thousand homes and sixteen thousand people, and the government, which tried to halt the construction because of where the money came from, does not legalize it for twenty-eight years. Residents still say, to anyone who asks, that he gave them somewhere to live.
stops.quote: Soy gran amigo y hago todo lo posible para que la gente me aprecie. Lo que más vale en la vida son los amigos.
stops.quote_source: Luis Cañón, 'El patron: vida y muerte de Pablo Escobar' (Planeta, 1994), p. 83, via es.wikiquote.org
suggested_refs: Municipal legalization file for the Loreto settlement, Comuna 9, Medellín, 15 August 2012

stops.name: Medellín, the club at the Atanasio Girardot
stops.date_confidence: attested in outline by en.wikipedia, 'Atlético Nacional', which carries Francisco Maturana's statement about narco money and the later CONMEBOL ban. The article debates how much of the money was Escobar's personally rather than the cartel's generally and does not itemize it. No year is attested for the money entering the club: the date here is a placeholder inside the 1980s, set after the Medellín sin Tugurios stop for ordering only, and month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: Cartel money goes into Atlético Nacional and the club can suddenly keep its players and buy foreign ones. The stadium in Laureles fills. In 1989 the team becomes the first Colombian side to win the Copa Libertadores, and the city celebrates in the street. CONMEBOL later bars Colombian clubs from hosting international matches, because referees are being threatened. Francisco Maturana, who managed the side, says afterward that the money let the club hold on to talent it could not otherwise have paid for.
suggested_refs: CONMEBOL disciplinary rulings on Colombian clubs and referee intimidation, late 1980s

stops.name: Bogotá, the retirement from politics
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month, January 1984, by en.wikipedia; day defaulted. Corrected from the verified pool: Galán rejected Escobar from Nuevo Liberalismo, his own faction, in 1982, not from the Liberal Party as a whole. Pin is the canonical generic Bogotá coordinate, not a located building.
stops.campa: Justice Minister Rodrigo Lara Bonilla stands up in the Congress and names where the alternate representative from Medellín gets his money. Nuevo Liberalismo has already turned him out; Luis Carlos Galán rejected him from the movement in 1982 in front of everyone. In January he announces that he is leaving politics. He does not announce that he is leaving anything else. The presidency he had described to his university friends is now shut to him by every legal road. He is thirty-four years old.
suggested_refs: Congressional record of Rodrigo Lara Bonilla's denunciations, Bogotá, 1983-1984

stops.name: Bogotá, the motorcycle on the Autopista Norte
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia, 'Rodrigo Lara Bonilla' gives the date, the Autopista Norte at Calle 127, the Mac-10 and the motorcycle, and traces the order to Escobar. 'Plata o plomo' is tagged [R]: it is universally attributed to him as the formula of his bribery-or-death ultimatums and no primary transcript of him saying it has been located.
stops.campa: Three months after the announced retirement, the Justice Minister's car is running north on the Autopista at Calle 127 when a motorcycle comes up alongside and a gunman empties a Mac-10 through the window. Lara Bonilla is thirty-seven years old. The method is the one the trade brought home from Miami, a pillion rider and a machine pistol at traffic speed, and it will be used on judges, journalists, policemen and candidates for the next nine years. The order is traced to Escobar and no court in Colombia ever tries him for it.
stops.quote_source: Universally attributed formula, carried by Colombia Reports and by guioteca.com's compilation; no primary transcript located [R]
suggested_refs: Colombian judicial file on the assassination of Rodrigo Lara Bonilla, 30 April 1984

stops.name: Bogotá, the Shaio clinic
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia, 'Rodrigo Lara Bonilla' records that he was pronounced dead minutes after arrival at the Shaio clinic. Coordinate corrected to the Fundación Clínica Shaio, Carrera 70D, Santa Rosa, Localidad Suba, per OpenStreetMap; the verified pool carried a value 3.8 km southeast, in Chapinero.
stops.campa: He is driven to the Shaio clinic in the north of the city and pronounced dead minutes after arrival. He is given a state funeral in the first days of May. The government of Belisario Betancur, which had held off extraditing anyone, begins extraditing. A state of siege comes down over the country. Within days Escobar and the Ochoas cross into Panama, and for the first time the cartel's leadership sleeps outside Colombia. The extradition the killing was meant to stop starts with the killing.
suggested_refs: Contemporary El Tiempo coverage of the Lara Bonilla state funeral, May 1984

stops.name: Panama City, the corridor across the isthmus
stops.date_confidence: contested, flagged not resolved. The Kerry Committee report states that associates of the Medellín cartel met Panamanian intermediaries close to General Noriega around 1984 to arrange transshipment and protection for refining laboratories; Noriega's memoir denies any such meeting flatly. Escobar's own personal presence at any meeting is nowhere established. Month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: In the months after the Lara killing the cartel's men look for ground the Colombian state cannot reach. The Kerry Committee report has associates of Escobar's organisation meeting intermediaries close to General Manuel Noriega, to arrange transshipment across the isthmus and protection for refining laboratories in the Darién. Noriega's own memoir denies flatly that any such meeting took place. In February 1988 a Miami grand jury indicts him for taking payment to let Colombian cocaine cross his country. The contradiction stands in the record unresolved.
sources: manuel_noriega.journey.json, stops 'Coclesito, the farm in the forest', 'Colon, the free zone at the other mouth' and 'Miami, the indictment'
Kerry Committee report on drugs, law enforcement and foreign policy (1988)
US v. Noriega trial record, S.D. Fla. 1992
suggested_refs: Kerry Committee hearings on the Panamanian transshipment corridor, 1988

stops.name: Bogotá, Los Extraditables
stops.date_confidence: attested to the season by en.wikipedia: in the fall of 1985 Escobar requested conditional surrender without extradition, the proposal was rejected, and he then founded Los Extraditables. Corrected from the verified pool, which spread this over 1984-1985. Month is the season's midpoint; day defaulted. Pin is the canonical generic Bogotá coordinate.
stops.campa: In the autumn he offers the government a conditional surrender: he will give himself up if he is not sent to the United States. The offer is refused. He and the other wanted traffickers then constitute themselves as Los Extraditables, a name that is also the whole of their demand. For the next six years the communiqués come out over that signature after each bomb, and they end on the same sentence: better a tomb in Colombia than a prison cell in the United States.
stops.quote: Better a tomb in Colombia than a prison cell in the United States.
stops.quote_source: biography.com, 'Pablo Escobar' (A&E Television Networks); Spanish phrasing corroborated on a guioteca.com compilation, original utterance untraced
suggested_refs: Surviving communiqués of Los Extraditables, 1985-1991, in Colombian press archives

stops.name: Bogotá, the Palace of Justice
stops.date_confidence: attested for the siege, contested for the financing. en.wikipedia, 'Palace of Justice siege' gives 6-7 November 1985, 101 dead and 11 of 25 justices killed; the verified pool's '98 dead' and 'nearly 100' both understate it and are corrected. Escobar's financing rests largely on Virginia Vallejo's testimony, and a 1986 Special Commission concluded that destroying files was not an M-19 objective.
stops.campa: M-19 guerrillas take the Palace of Justice on the Plaza de Bolívar with the Supreme Court sitting inside. The army retakes the building with tanks over two days. A hundred and one people are dead when it ends, eleven of the twenty-five justices among them, and the extradition files held in the building burn. That the cartel paid for the assault is asserted by Virginia Vallejo and believed by investigators; a Special Commission concluded in 1986 that destroying the files was not an objective of the M-19 at all. The charge has never been proved.
suggested_refs: Report of the 1986 Special Commission on the Palace of Justice siege

stops.name: Medellín, the bomb under the Monaco
stops.date_confidence: attested; es.wikipedia, 'Edificio Mónaco' gives 13 January 1988, an 80 kg dynamite charge in a grey Toyota on the order of Pacho Herrera of the Cali cartel, and the permanent damage to Manuela Escobar's hearing. Upgraded from [R] in the verified pool. Coordinate corrected to 6 degrees 11 minutes 29 seconds north, 75 degrees 34 minutes 41 seconds west, Santa María de los Ángeles; the pool's value fell 2.3 km north. Storey count is disputed: es.wikipedia says eight, en.wikipedia says six.
stops.campa: A grey Toyota loaded with eighty kilograms of dynamite goes off under the Mónaco building in Santa María de los Ángeles, where Escobar keeps his family and his paintings. The order comes from Pacho Herrera of the Cali cartel. Escobar is not in the building. His daughter Manuela is, and the blast takes her hearing for good. The war between Medellín and Cali starts here, and it will be Cali money that pays the men who eventually run him down. The sources cannot agree whether the building had six floors or eight.
suggested_refs: Medellín police report on the Edificio Mónaco car bomb, 13 January 1988

stops.name: Rionegro, the Procurador General on the road
stops.date_confidence: attested for the killing, reconstruction for the attribution. es.wikipedia, 'Carlos Mauro Hoyos' gives the kidnapping on 25 January 1988 near the José María Córdova airport and the body at the finca San Gerardo beside the vía Las Palmas, in Rionegro. The verified pool placed it in Guarne, which is the wrong municipality, and gave his title as Attorney General rather than Procurador General; both corrected. The attribution to Escobar's men rests on the sicario John Jairo Velásquez's testimony.
stops.campa: Twelve days after the Mónaco bomb, the Procurador General de la Nación, Carlos Mauro Hoyos, is taken on the road from Medellín to the airport at Rionegro and killed the same day. His body is found the same day at the finca San Gerardo, beside the vía Las Palmas. The attribution to Escobar's men rests on the later testimony of one of his own sicarios, and on nothing filed in a court. Hoyos was the officer of the republic charged with prosecuting exactly this. It is the municipality Escobar was born in, and the road to the airport runs past the town. He is thirty-eight years old.
stops.quote: Yo tengo 38 años de edad. 28 años fui pobre y me transportaba en buses.
stops.quote_source: es.wikiquote.org, 'Pablo Escobar', citing an unidentified YouTube video whose linked ID is malformed and dead as written; no broadcast, programme, interviewer or date given [R]
suggested_refs: Testimony of John Jairo Velásquez Vasquez on the Hoyos killing

stops.name: Soacha, the plaza and the candidate
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia, 'Luis Carlos Galán' gives 18 August 1989, the Soacha rally, roughly ten thousand present, eighteen bodyguards and warnings against making the trip, and attributes the plot to Escobar together with Gonzalo Rodríguez Gacha and Alberto Santofimio, who was convicted in 2007.
stops.campa: Luis Carlos Galán, front-runner for the presidency, the man who threw him out of Nuevo Liberalismo seven years earlier, climbs onto a platform in the plaza at Soacha in front of ten thousand people. He has eighteen bodyguards and has been warned not to come. Eighteen years later a court will convict the politician Alberto Santofimio for his part in the planning, alongside Escobar and Gonzalo Rodríguez Gacha. On the night itself the gunmen are standing inside the crowd, among the ten thousand, and they fire at the platform from there.
suggested_refs: 2007 conviction of Alberto Santofimio for the Galán assassination

stops.name: Soacha, Avianca 203 comes down
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia, 'Avianca Flight 203' gives the bomb five minutes after takeoff, all 107 aboard and three on the ground killed, and César Gaviria as the intended target though he was not on the aircraft. Coordinate is the municipality the wreckage fell across, not a single crash point.
stops.campa: Five minutes out of Bogotá a bomb goes off in the cabin of a Boeing 727 bound for Cali and the aircraft comes apart in the air over Soacha, the same municipality where Galán was shot three months before. All hundred and seven people aboard are killed and three more on the ground. The target is the candidate César Gaviria, who is not on the flight and was never booked on it. Two of the dead are American citizens, and from that point the United States is in the hunt directly, with its own men and its own equipment.
suggested_refs: Colombian and US investigative files on the bombing of Avianca Flight 203

stops.name: Bogotá, the DAS building
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia, 'DAS Building bombing' gives an estimated 9,000 kg of dynamite, 63 killed, more than 2,200 injured, and the failed attempt on director Miguel Maza Márquez. The verified pool's chronology lens had flagged this date as unconfirmed; the dedicated article confirms it.
stops.campa: A truck carrying an estimated nine thousand kilograms of dynamite is driven up to the headquarters of the DAS, the state security service, in the centre of Bogotá, and detonated. Sixty-three people are killed and more than two thousand two hundred injured. Blocks of the city come down. The director, Miguel Maza Márquez, who is what the charge was brought for, walks out of the wreck of his own building alive. Nine days have passed since the airliner came apart over Soacha.
stops.quote: [Terrorism is] the atomic bomb for poor people. It is the only way for the poor to strike back.
stops.quote_source: biography.com, 'Pablo Escobar' (A&E Television Networks); no interview date given, primary transcript not located
suggested_refs: DAS internal investigation into the 6 December 1989 bombing

stops.name: Bogotá, the clause in the constitution
stops.date_confidence: attested that the 1991 constitution banned extradition of Colombian nationals and that the ban is widely believed to reflect Escobar's pressure, per en.wikipedia. The 4 July 1991 date is the constitution's promulgation and is supplied here for ordering; no source consulted ties a specific vote date to Escobar. Pin is the canonical generic Bogotá coordinate.
stops.campa: The Constituent Assembly writes Colombia a new constitution and puts into it a prohibition on extraditing Colombian nationals. The delegates deny that anyone leaned on them. Los Extraditables have spent six years bombing, kidnapping and killing toward precisely this clause, and the clause is in the finished text. Escobar surrenders within weeks of it. Whether the assembly was bought, frightened, or simply worn down along with the rest of a country sick of car bombs, nobody has established.
suggested_refs: Debates of the 1991 Colombian Constituent Assembly on the extradition clause

stops.name: Envigado, the prison he builds
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year and the arrangement by en.wikipedia, 'La Catedral', which describes the negotiated surrender shielding him from extradition, the football pitch, bar, jacuzzi, waterfall and telescope. June is given for the surrender by the verified pool's geography lens; day defaulted. The quote is tagged [R]: an unsourced listicle line with no traceable original.
stops.campa: He gives himself up to the state on the condition that he not be extradited, and is confined in a prison he has built himself on a hillside above Envigado, on land he owns, guarded by men he has chosen. It has a football pitch, a bar, a jacuzzi and a waterfall. He runs the cartel from inside it by telephone and receives whom he likes, and the government of César Gaviria calls this an imprisonment, and for thirteen months everybody agrees to call it that. There is also a telescope, set up on the hillside and trained down the valley on the house where his family sleeps.
stops.quote: A veces yo soy Dios. Si digo que un hombre muere, muere el mismo día.
stops.quote_source: guioteca.com listicle of phrases attributed to Escobar (23 June 2017); no interview, letter or trial cited [R]
suggested_refs: Terms of the 1991 surrender agreement between Escobar and the government of César Gaviria

stops.name: Envigado, Galeano and Moncada come up the hill
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia, 'La Catedral' records the torture and murder of Fernando Galeano and Gerardo Moncada inside the prison over a dispute about cartel money, and the transfer order that followed. Day within July not fixed by the source and defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Two of his own lieutenants, Fernando Galeano and Gerardo Moncada, come up the hill to answer a question about money and are tortured and killed inside the prison. Word of it goes down to Bogotá within days. The fiction that the man in La Catedral is in state custody cannot survive a double murder committed inside the walls by the prisoner himself, and the government orders him moved to a military barracks. Somebody inside the arrangement tells him before the order arrives.
suggested_refs: Colombian prosecution file on the Galeano and Moncada killings at La Catedral

stops.name: Envigado, out through the wall
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia, 'La Catedral' gives 22 July 1992, the walk out through a pre-weakened section of wall, and roughly one year and one month served. The site has been run as a Benedictine monastery since 2007, per the same article.
stops.campa: Forewarned, he and his men walk out through a section of wall left weak when the place was put up, on the twenty-second of July, one year and one month after he came in. The soldiers sent to move him arrive at an empty prison and are photographed standing in it. He is forty-two years old and will not sleep in the same house twice again. Since 2007 Benedictine monks have kept the buildings as a monastery, and the road up the hill carries visitors on weekends.
suggested_refs: The surviving structures of La Catedral, Envigado, in Benedictine use since 2007

stops.name: Medellín, Los Pepes
stops.date_confidence: attested for the group's composition and conduct by en.wikipedia, 'Los Pepes', which gives an active span of 1992-1993 and no founding date. Corrected from the verified pool, which dated the group flat to 1992: the campaign followed the July 1992 escape and ran chiefly through 1993. August 1992 is an ordering device, not an attested founding.
stops.campa: In the aftermath of the escape a group forms calling itself Los Pepes, Perseguidos por Pablo Escobar, led by the Castaño brothers and paid for by the Cali cartel. Through 1993 they kill his lawyers, his accountants, his drivers and his guards. What they learn they hand to the state's Search Bloc, and the Search Bloc hands back what it learns. The method being used against him is the method he invented, and it is running faster than his did. They blow up his family's properties, and they burn two haciendas belonging to his mother Hermilda.
suggested_refs: Human Rights Watch, 'State of War: Political Violence and Counterinsurgency in Colombia' (1993)

stops.name: Medellín, the accountant gives himself up
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, flagged not resolved. en.wikipedia, 'Roberto Escobar' says he escaped La Catedral with Pablo in July 1992 and surrendered 'a year later', i.e. around mid-1993, with no place given; the background dossier had him surrendering to US authorities in 1996, a version with no retrievable support. Date here follows the Wikipedia reading. The memoir is 'The Accountant's Story' (Grand Central, 2009), not 'The Accountant' (2010) as the pool had it.
stops.campa: Roberto Escobar, called El Osito, the cartel's accountant and his brother, who went over the wall of La Catedral beside him, gives himself up about a year after the escape. In prison a letter bomb takes an eye and most of his hearing. In 2009 he publishes an account of the whole business under his own name. On the year of the surrender the sources do not agree, one giving 1993 and one 1996, and neither records a place; the earlier reading is followed here because it is the one attached to a stated interval.
sources: Roberto Escobar, 'The Accountant's Story: Inside the Violent World of the Medellín Cartel' (Grand Central, 2009)
suggested_refs: Roberto Escobar, 'The Accountant's Story' (2009)

stops.name: Medellín, the roof at Los Olivos
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia, 'Death of Pablo Escobar' gives 2 December 1993, the Los Olivos neighbourhood, the bodyguard Álvaro de Jesús Agudelo ('Limón'), the day after his forty-fourth birthday, and the unresolved question of the fatal shot. Coordinate corrected to 6 degrees 15 minutes 13.6 seconds north, 75 degrees 35 minutes 52.4 seconds west; the verified pool's value sat 1.3 km east.
stops.campa: He is traced by his own voice on a radio telephone to a house in Los Olivos, a middle-class neighbourhood of Medellín, the day after his forty-fourth birthday. The Search Bloc surrounds the block, with American equipment behind them. He and his bodyguard Álvaro de Jesús Agudelo, called Limón, go out over the tiles of the roof in stocking feet and are shot there. Whether the wound behind his ear came from a police rifle or from his own pistol has never been settled, and his son argues to this day for the second.
stops.quote: My father's not a person to be imitated. He showed us the path we must never take as a society because it's the path to self-destruction, the loss of values, and a place where life ceases to have importance.
stops.quote_source: Sebastián Marroquín (Juan Pablo Escobar), quoted by biography.com, 'Pablo Escobar' (A&E Television Networks)
suggested_refs: Sebastián Marroquín, 'Pablo Escobar: My Father' (2014)

segments.name: Montesacro and What Grew From It

stops.name: Itagüí, the burial at Jardines Montesacro
stops.date_confidence: attested for the burial, the cemetery and the estimated 25,000 mourners, per en.wikipedia, 'Death of Pablo Escobar'. Coordinate inherited byte-identically from griselda_blanco.journey.json so that the two graves share one pin; note that OpenStreetMap places Jardines Montesacro at 6.1604, -75.6205 and two other lenses of the research pool gave two further values. The discrepancy is flagged, not silently resolved.
stops.campa: He is buried the next day at Jardines Montesacro in Itagüí, in the family plot where his mother and his brother will follow him. Griselda Blanco, who opened the Miami routes his cartel took over and whose name the cartel's fame eclipsed, is buried a hundred paces off on the same lawn in 2012, and coaches now stop for both. An estimated twenty-five thousand people come to the funeral, most of them out of the comunas, and at the graveside the lid is taken off the coffin so that they can see his face.
stops.quote: He built houses and cared about the poor. In the future, people will go to his tomb to pray, the way they would to a saint.
stops.quote_source: An unnamed mourner at Escobar's funeral, 3 December 1993, quoted by biography.com, 'Pablo Escobar' (A&E Television Networks)
sources: griselda_blanco.journey.json, stop 'Jardines Montesacro, Itagüí: a hundred paces from Escobar'
suggested_refs: Contemporary El Colombiano and El Tiempo coverage of the funeral, 3 December 1993

stops.name: Itagüí, the grave opened
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia, 'Pablo Escobar' gives 28 October 2006, the DNA sample taken for a paternity claim by a man asserting to be an illegitimate son, the RCN broadcast, and Sebastián Marroquín's anger at the filming. The result of the paternity test is not reported in any source consulted, and is recorded here as a gap.
stops.campa: Thirteen years on, the grave is opened at the family's own request so that a DNA sample can be taken, a man having come forward claiming to be his son. The network RCN films the exhumation and broadcasts it to the country. Sebastián Marroquín, the son nobody disputes, objects publicly to the filming and gets nowhere. The skull is handled on camera, thirteen years in the ground, by men in gloves. What the paternity test showed is given in no published source located.
suggested_refs: RCN broadcast footage of the 28 October 2006 exhumation

stops.name: Medellín, the barrio legalized
stops.date_confidence: attested; es.wikipedia, 'Barrio Pablo Escobar' gives the growth to 443 dwellings, then roughly 4,000 homes and 16,000 residents by 2011, and legalization on 15 August 2012. Coordinate corrected to Comuna 9 (Buenos Aires) per OpenStreetMap.
stops.campa: Twenty-eight years after the first two hundred and fifty houses go up, and nineteen after the man who paid for them is shot off a roof, the Colombian state legalizes the neighbourhood. Sixteen thousand people are living in it by then. The paperwork records it as Loreto. Journalists have been coming for three decades to ask the residents about the other name. On the walls of the neighbourhood the murals carry his face, and the name the people living there use is Barrio Pablo Escobar.
suggested_refs: Municipal legalization decree for the Loreto settlement, Medellín, 15 August 2012

stops.name: Medellín, the Mónaco comes down
stops.date_confidence: attested with a date conflict flagged. en.wikipedia, 'Pablo Escobar' gives 22 February 2019 at 11:53 AM local time and both the chronology and geography lenses of the research pool agree; es.wikipedia, 'Edificio Mónaco' gives 24 February. The timestamped record is preferred here and the conflict is left standing rather than resolved.
stops.campa: At 11:53 in the morning the charges bring the Mónaco building down. It is the block where he kept his family and his paintings, and where the Cali cartel put eighty kilograms of dynamite in January 1988 without bringing it down. The Spanish and English records of the demolition differ by two days on the date, and nobody has reconciled them. The mayor's office stages it as the removal of a symbol, and on the cleared ground it lays out a memorial park for the victims of the cartel.
suggested_refs: Medellín municipal programme for the Parque Memorial Inflexion on the Mónaco site

stops.name: Puerto Triunfo, the hippopotamuses in the Magdalena
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia, "Pablo Escobar's hippos" gives four hippos imported in 1981, 40 by 2014, 90 to 120 by 2019, 181 to 215 in 2023 and around two hundred in 2026, GonaCon sterilization under way by October 2021, and Ministry of Environment approval on 13 April 2026 to euthanize more than eighty at a cost of 7.2 billion pesos. Head-counts move between sources and should be read as estimates.
stops.campa: The estate is seized after his death. The zoo animals are dispersed to South American facilities, except four hippopotamuses brought in from abroad in 1981, which nobody can work out how to move. In the warm water of the Magdalena they breed with nothing to stop them: forty by 2014, around two hundred by 2026. The government starts sterilizing them with GonaCon in 2021 and in April 2026 approves killing more than eighty. Part of the grounds has run as a theme park since 2014, with a water park and a safari tour.
suggested_refs: Colombian Ministry of Environment resolution of 13 April 2026 on the Magdalena hippopotamus population

stops.name: Medellín, the tomb people pray at
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. en.wikipedia states the folk-saint veneration as fact but names no ethnographic source and does not quantify it; the funeral quotation from biography.com is the strongest single piece of evidence for the register. The Casa Museo in El Poblado could not be confirmed this pass, its dedicated article returning 404. The devotion is continuous from December 1993; the date carried here is not an event but a terminal ordering device, placed at the end of the file's clock so that the standing condition closes the sequence.
stops.campa: In the comunas he built in, people pray to him. The devotion is reported and never counted: no shrine is catalogued, no liturgy is written down, and the Church has nothing to say about it. In 2015 a series told the story again in English through the eyes of a DEA agent, and Colombians objected to the accents and the framing, and the tours grew longer. Tours run daily now to the houses he lived in, hid in and died in, and to a museum his family keeps in El Poblado. Cocaine is sold to the people who come on them.
suggested_refs: Ethnographic studies of popular veneration of Escobar in Medellín's comunas, none located this pass
